claims.text: The initial HEA is a uniform, single-phase solid solution.
HEA deformation behavior can depend on temperature and strain rate.
High-strain-rate and/or low-temperature loading produces local stress-induced instabilities in the HEA.
The loading-induced instabilities nucleate brittle intermetallic precipitates.
The loading-induced instabilities initiate microcracks at grain boundaries.
Brittle precipitates and/or grain-boundary microcracks reduce toughness and cause a ductile-to-brittle fracture transition.
The governing behavior can be tested by systematically varying strain rate and temperature while holding alloy composition constant.
High strain rates, cyclic or shock loading, and cryogenic temperatures are the applicable demanding-service regimes.
Accumulated dislocations and grain-boundary stress concentrations overcome local energy barriers under demanding loading.
Overcoming these local energy barriers promotes phase decomposition or precipitation of brittle constituents.
The resulting local phase instability disrupts the single-phase structure and reduces plastic deformation capacity and toughness.
Under moderate baseline loading, the HEA deforms homogeneously and fails by ductile dimpled fracture with high toughness and no detectable brittle secondary phases.
High-strain-rate or low-temperature loading will cause a marked toughness decrease relative to the moderate-condition baseline.
The extreme-condition specimens will exhibit cleavage-type brittle fracture surfaces.
Post-mortem characterization of extreme-condition specimens will reveal secondary brittle phases or microcrack networks.
A loading threshold separates preservation of the homogeneous single-phase structure from loading-induced structural instability.
The exact strain-rate and temperature thresholds and the composition, size, and distribution of any brittle phase are unknown.

The hypothesis is falsified if extreme-condition specimens show neither a statistically significant toughness reduction nor brittle-phase precipitation or microcrack formation relative to the baseline.
